random experiment: Any procedure whose specific outcome cannot be predicted: a die roll, a card draw, a coin flip. Its possible outcomes form the sample space. See [Random experiments, sample spaces, events](#/math3042-u3/probability-sample-space).
sample space|S: The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, e.g. $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ for one die or the 36 pairs for two dice. Written $S$; the classical probability of an event is $|A|/|S|$ when the outcomes are equally likely. See [Random experiments, sample spaces, events](#/math3042-u3/probability-sample-space).
event|A: Any subset of the sample space, such as 'exactly one head' = {HTT, THT, TTH}. See [Random experiments, sample spaces, events](#/math3042-u3/probability-sample-space).
random variable|X: A numerical value $X$ that depends on the outcome of a random experiment: the number of heads, the sum of two dice, the number of red cards drawn. See [Random experiments, sample spaces, events](#/math3042-u3/probability-sample-space).
classical probability: $P(A) = |A| / |S|$ when every outcome in $S$ is equally likely; between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). See [Random experiments, sample spaces, events](#/math3042-u3/probability-sample-space).
relative frequency: $P(A) \approx x/n$: the fraction of $n$ trials in which $A$ occurred; the basis of every Lab 4 simulation. See [Relative frequency and the law of large numbers](#/math3042-u3/relative-frequency-lln).
law of large numbers: If the experiment is performed enough times, the relative frequency $x/n$ must approach the exact classical probability $P(A)$. See [Relative frequency and the law of large numbers](#/math3042-u3/relative-frequency-lln).
boxcars: Both dice showing six in Craps: one of 36 equally likely outcomes, $P = 1/36 = 0.0278$, simulated in the notes with a for loop and `sample()`. See [Relative frequency and the law of large numbers](#/math3042-u3/relative-frequency-lln).
fundamental counting rule|counting rule: With $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$ choices at each step there are $n_1 \times n_2 \times \cdots \times n_k$ outcomes in all: $6^5 = 7776$ for five die rolls. See [The counting rule, permutations and combinations](#/math3042-u3/counting).
factorial|n!: $n! = n(n-1)\cdots 2 \cdot 1$, the number of ways to arrange $n$ distinct items in a sequence: $4! = 24$ for the four Aces. R: `factorial(4)`. See [The counting rule, permutations and combinations](#/math3042-u3/counting).
permutation|permutations|P(n, r)|nPr: $P(n, r) = n!/(n-r)!$: the number of **ordered** sequences of $r$ items chosen from $n$ without repeats, e.g. $P(52, 4) = 6\,497\,400$. Calculator key `nPr`; R: `choose(n, r) * factorial(r)`. See [The counting rule, permutations and combinations](#/math3042-u3/counting).
combination|combinations|C(n, r)|nCr: $C(n, r) = n! / (r!\,(n-r)!) = P(n, r)/r!$: the number of **unordered** groups (hands, committees) of $r$ from $n$, e.g. $C(52, 4) = 270\,725$. Calculator key `nCr`; R: `choose(n, r)`. See [The counting rule, permutations and combinations](#/math3042-u3/counting).
with replacement|replace=TRUE: Each item is returned before the next draw, so draws are independent and values may repeat: dice, coins, `sample(x, n, replace=TRUE)`. Probabilities multiply without changing. See [The counting rule, permutations and combinations](#/math3042-u3/counting).
without replacement: Each draw removes an item, so later probabilities change: two Aces are $(4/52)(3/51)$, and `sample(deck, n)` without `replace=TRUE`. See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
complement|complement rule: $\bar{A} = S - A$ is everything in $S$ not in $A$, and $P(\bar{A}) = 1 - P(A)$. Use it for 'at least one' and 'less than the maximum'. See [The complement and addition rules](#/math3042-u3/complement-addition).
birthday problem: Among 23 people, $P(\text{at least two share a birthday}) = 1 - P(365, 23)/365^{23} = 1 - 0.4927 = 0.5073$, by the complement rule; the demo notebook's simulation gives about 0.507. See [The complement and addition rules](#/math3042-u3/complement-addition).
addition rule: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$: the overlap is subtracted so it is not counted twice. For mutually exclusive events it is $P(A) + P(B)$. See [The complement and addition rules](#/math3042-u3/complement-addition).
mutually exclusive: Two events that cannot both occur in one trial (a black card and a heart): $P(A \cap B) = 0$. Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are always dependent. See [The complement and addition rules](#/math3042-u3/complement-addition).
conditional probability: $P(B \mid A) = |A \cap B| / |A| = P(A \cap B)/P(A)$: the probability of $B$ when the sample space is restricted to $A$. On a two-way table, a cell over its row or column total. See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
two-way table: A table of counts with one categorical variable on the rows and another on the columns (handedness by phone type, $n = 71$): row and column totals give marginal probabilities, cells over totals give conditional ones. See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
independent|independence: Events with $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$, equivalently $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$: knowing $A$ does not change the probability of $B$. Right-handed and iPhone in the notes are dependent ($0.732 \ne 0.702$). See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
multiplication rule: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$ in general, $P(A)\,P(B)$ when independent: two Aces are $1/169$ with replacement and $1/221$ without. See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
exhaustive: Events $A_1, \ldots, A_k$ are exhaustive and mutually exclusive when together they cover the whole sample space without overlapping (female/male; Intel/AMD/Other). See [Bayes' rule on a tree diagram](#/math3042-u3/bayes).
law of total probability|total probabili: $P(B) = \sum_i P(A_i)\,P(B \mid A_i)$: add every path of the tree that ends in $B$; $P(\text{defective}) = 0.0085 + 0.0030 + 0.0010 = 0.0125$. See [Bayes' rule on a tree diagram](#/math3042-u3/bayes).
Bayes' rule|Bayes' theorem|Bayes: $P(A_i \mid B) = P(A_i)\,P(B \mid A_i) / \sum_j P(A_j)\,P(B \mid A_j)$: reverses a conditional probability by dividing one path of the tree by the total probability of $B$; $P(\text{Intel} \mid \text{defective}) = 0.0085/0.0125 = 0.68$. See [Bayes' rule on a tree diagram](#/math3042-u3/bayes).
tree diagram: First-level branches carry the priors $P(A_i)$, second-level branches the conditionals $P(B \mid A_i)$; multiplying along a path gives a joint probability. See [Bayes' rule on a tree diagram](#/math3042-u3/bayes).
survey: The MASS data frame of 237 statistics students (Sex, W.Hnd, Wr.Hnd, NW.Hnd, Height, Pulse, …) used throughout Lab 3. See [Lab 3: charts of the survey data](#/math3042-u3/lab3-charts-r).
paste0|paste0(): Glues strings and numbers with no separator, element by element: `paste0("Writing Hand of Students (n = ", sum(freq.tab), ")")` builds a title from the data instead of hard-coding $n$. See [Lab 3: charts of the survey data](#/math3042-u3/lab3-charts-r).
cut|cut(): `cut(x, breaks, right=FALSE)` assigns each value to a class labelled `[lower, upper)`; `table()` of the result is the frequency distribution and `cumsum()` the cumulative one. See [Lab 3: charts of the survey data](#/math3042-u3/lab3-charts-r).
sample|sample()|sample.int: `sample(x, n, replace=TRUE, prob=)` draws $n$ values from `x`; `sample.int(6, n, replace=TRUE)` rolls $n$ dice. `replace=TRUE` allows repeats (dice, coins); omit it for cards; `prob=` loads the die. See [Lab 4: simulating probabilities](#/math3042-u3/lab4-simulations).
replicate|replicate(): `replicate(m, expr)` evaluates `expr` $m$ times and returns the results as a vector, replacing a for loop whose body ignores its index. See [Lab 4: simulating probabilities](#/math3042-u3/lab4-simulations).
for loop|for: `for (i in 1:m) { res[i] <- ... }` runs the body once per value of `i`; allocate `numeric(m)` or `character(m)` first to store results. See [Lab 4: simulating probabilities](#/math3042-u3/lab4-simulations).
function|function(): `name <- function(args) { ...; return(value) }` defines an R function such as `Prob.Heads(m)` or `Roll.Some.Dice(m, n)`. See [Lab 4: simulating probabilities](#/math3042-u3/lab4-simulations).
prop.table|prop.table(): Turns a table of counts into relative frequencies; `barplot(prop.table(table(die.vals)))` is Lab 4's bar plot of $X$. See [Lab 4: simulating probabilities](#/math3042-u3/lab4-simulations).
